sections.title: BACKGROUND

summary.text: Sets out the main causes of illness and death in children with HIV in low- and middle-income countries, such as pneumonia, TB and malnutrition, and explains that the brief builds on WHO's 2017 advanced HIV disease guidelines. It notes that many interventions also apply to children without advanced disease.

sections.extract: The major causes of morbidity and mortality among children living with HIV in low- and middle-income countries are pneumonia (including Pneumocystis pneumonia), tuberculosis (TB), bloodstream infections, diarrhoeal disease and severe acute malnutrition (1,2). In addition, for adolescents living with HIV, adult-type opportunistic infections also occur, including cryptococcal meningitis (3,4). WHO published guidelines

sections.title: Current WHO guidelines on managing advanced HIV disease

summary.text: Summarizes WHO's 2017 guidance on advanced HIV disease, defining it for children and noting that all children under five are considered to have advanced disease, with exceptions for those stable on treatment. It explains that the evidence base comes mainly from adult trials such as REMSTART and REALITY. It then outlines the screening, prophylaxis and treatment recommendations relevant to children and adolescents, including that cryptococcal screening is not advised under age 10.

sections.extract: advanced HIV disease In 2017, WHO published guidelines for managing advanced HIV disease and rapid initiation of antiretroviral therapy (5). Advanced HIV disease is defined as WHO stage 3 or 4 or a CD4 cell count <200 cells/mm3 for children five years or older. All children younger than five years are considered to have advanced disease (5). This is based on the rationale that most children younger than five years

sections.title: Tuberculosis

summary.text: Describes the high incidence of TB in children with HIV and the symptoms used to screen for it, noting the overlap with other HIV-related signs. It covers the limits of urine LF-LAM testing in children, the 2019 LAM recommendations and the advantages of rapid molecular tests such as Xpert MTB/RIF, while stressing the continuing role of clinical diagnosis.

sections.extract: The incidence of TB in a cohort of children living with HIV in Uganda and Zimbabwe ranged from 1.2 to 8.8 per 100 child-years, and an estimated 15% of children starting antiretroviral therapy in sub-Saharan Africa develop TB (14,15). Although antiretroviral therapy reduces children’s risk of TB infection, its full protective potential is only evident 1–2 years after starting antiretroviral therapy (8). TB is

sections.title: Cryptococcal disease

summary.text: Explains that cryptococcal disease is rare in young children with HIV, so antigen screening is recommended only for adolescents, and lists useful WHO resources on TB diagnostics and HIV guidelines.

sections.extract: In contrast to adults, cryptococcal disease is rare, especially among children younger than five years of age. In a laboratory-based survey performed in South Africa, the incidence of cryptococcal disease was estimated to be 47 per 100 000 children living with HIV in 2007 (26), and within two trial cohorts of children living with HIV, no cases of cryptococcal disease were reported for children younger than five

sections.title: Tuberculosis

summary.text: Describes child-friendly fixed-dose TB treatment formulations and how to manage drug interactions between rifampicin and lopinavir/ritonavir or dolutegravir in children with HIV.

sections.extract: Treatment for drug-sensitive TB among children comprises a four-drug regimen that includes rifampicin (R), isoniazid (H), pyrazinamide (Z) and ethambutol (E). A child-friendly, fixed- dose combination, dispersible tablet of RHZ is available and can be taken with a 100-mg child friendly formulation of E (intensive-phase treatment). In addition, there is a child-friendly, dispersible fixed-dose combination of RH for

sections.title: Severe pneumonia

summary.text: Covers the bacterial causes of severe pneumonia in children with HIV, classification by IMCI algorithms and high-dose co-trimoxazole for suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia in young infants. It notes that for children aged one to five, standard WHO antibiotics are preferred over co-trimoxazole.

sections.extract: In studies of severe pneumonia among children living with HIV, the most common bacterial pathogens isolated were predominantly Streptococcus pneumoniae and Staphylococcus aureus, pathogens that may be effectively covered by commonly available and recommended antibacterial medications (29). sections.title: Severe bacterial infections

summary.text: Describes high rates of bacteraemia in children starting antiretroviral therapy and the pathogens involved, advising treatment according to WHO guidelines.

sections.extract: High rates of bacteraemia have been described in children starting antiretroviral therapy, especially within the first three months of treatment (35,36). A recent study of 82 children with malnutrition admitted to a tertiary hospital in Durban, South Africa showed that 6% of admission blood cultures were positive. Community-associated infections were primarily Streptococcus or Staphylococcus. Health care-associated

sections.title: Cryptococcal meningitis

summary.text: Gives the preferred one-week amphotericin B and flucytosine induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis in children with HIV.

sections.extract: Guidelines for cryptococcal meningitis treatment have been revised, and a short-course (one- week) induction regimen with amphotericin B deoxycholate (1.0 mg/kg per day) and flucytosine (100 mg/kg per day, divided into four doses per day) is the preferred option for children living with HIV. Further recommendations are available in the 2018 WHO guidelines (13).

sections.title: Malnutrition

summary.text: Notes that severe acute malnutrition is common and deadly at HIV diagnosis and that malnutrition treatment should be part of children's HIV programmes. It then lists useful resources on child TB formulations, pneumonia management and malnutrition.

sections.extract: Severe acute malnutrition is common at HIV diagnosis and carries a high risk of mortality. The availability of malnutrition treatment programmes and commodities, including ready- to-use therapeutic food where appropriate, can be considered as essential components of HIV treatment programmes for children. sections.title: OPTIMIZE

summary.text: Reviews trials from South Africa and Kenya on the timing of antiretroviral therapy in children with severe acute malnutrition or hospitalization. It also stresses the risk of loss to follow-up and the need to link children to ongoing HIV care at discharge.

sections.extract: In a randomized trial from South Africa, young children living with HIV (median age 23 months) with severe acute malnutrition were randomized to receive antiretroviral therapy within 14 days of admission or for antiretroviral therapy to be delayed until nutritional recovery (and after two weeks; median time 23 days) (39). The results suggested that a short delay in antiretroviral therapy initiation during early

sections.title: Counselling and support

summary.text: Calls for more counselling and adolescent-friendly adherence support with earlier treatment initiation, and lists counselling resources.

sections.extract: Additional counselling and support are needed with earlier antiretroviral therapy initiation. Counselling tools have been updated to reflect newer optimal regimens and formulations. Adolescents generally face challenges in adhering to medication, and adolescent- friendly services, including enhanced adherence counselling, adolescent peer counsellors and support groups, may be especially valuable. Useful resources

sections.title: Preventing TB, Pneumocystis pneumonia, bacterial infections and cryptococcal disease

summary.text: Covers TB preventive treatment for children with HIV, including the restricted use in infants without a TB contact and the preferred six-month isoniazid regimen with pyridoxine. It describes shorter rifampicin- or rifapentine-based options, their interactions with antiretroviral drugs in a summary table, and related resources.

sections.extract: bacterial infections and cryptococcal disease Tuberculosis TB preventive treatment has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality among children living with HIV one year and older even if they do not have a known TB contact (41). Despite this, TB preventive treatment has not yet been fully implemented as part of comprehensive HIV care for children and adolescents (42). TB preventive treatment is currently not

sections.title: PCP and other infections

summary.text: Reviews evidence on co-trimoxazole prophylaxis to prevent Pneumocystis pneumonia and other infections in children with HIV and when it may be stopped. It also addresses fluconazole and cryptococcal antigen screening for adolescents, including lumbar puncture for those who test positive.

sections.extract: Co-trimoxazole Studies done in South Africa and Zambia in the era before antiretroviral therapy showed a high prevalence of Pneumocystis pneumonia, with infants younger than six months being especially vulnerable regardless of CD4 cell count (44,45). Despite improved access to antiretroviral therapy, Pneumocystis pneumonia remains a common cause of hospitalization because of undiagnosed HIV among infants.

sections.title: Vaccinations

summary.text: Sets out vaccination guidance for children with HIV, focusing on BCG, human papillomavirus, measles and pneumococcal vaccines, including timing relative to antiretroviral therapy and immune recovery. It notes differences in BCG practice between countries and gives revaccination and catch-up advice. A case study describes scaling up the advanced HIV disease package for children in Malawi using a hub-and-spoke model and the challenges encountered.

sections.extract: The WHO 2017 advanced HIV disease guidelines (5) highlighted the importance of vaccination in preventing severe disease among people living with HIV. Several other important vaccines were specifically recommended, including meningococcal, polio, rotavirus and yellow fever; however, this publication focuses on immunizations for the vaccine-preventable infections that are most significant to children living with HIV:

sections.title: National level

summary.text: Lists national-level implementation steps, such as adopting the guidelines, aligning HIV, TB and child health guidance, procuring child formulations and enabling catch-up vaccination.

sections.title: Facility level

summary.text: Lists facility-level considerations for the paediatric advanced HIV disease package, including hub-and-spoke delivery, task shifting, child-friendly settings and equipment. It also stresses functioning referral systems, for example for safe administration of amphotericin B.

sections.extract: ■Currently, the advanced HIV disease package is being implemented as a hub-and-spoke model. Further guidance on this is available in the global advanced HIV disease toolkit (http://www. differentiatedcare.org/Resources/Resource-Library/Global-Advanced-HIV-DiseaseToolkit). ■In the context of ongoing and enhanced efforts to ensure task shifting for services for children, all cadres of health-care workers need training

sections.title: Health-care providers

summary.text: Lists actions for health-care providers, such as training on child health issues and paediatric TB screening, and stresses that clinical diagnosis and treatment of TB should continue when tests are unavailable or negative.

sections.extract: ■Health-care providers should be sensitized on child-specific issues such as growth monitoring and other routine child health interventions. ■Training and capacity building for staff should be implemented in sites where these recommendations are to be implemented. ■Ensure that the advanced HIV disease package is included in any curriculum of training on HIV related to children or adolescents. ■Uptake of TB screening

sections.title: Laboratory

summary.text: Calls for laboratory procedures for collecting specimens from young children and for antibiotic resistance surveillance.

sections.extract: ■Ensure that protocols and standard operating procedures are in place for obtaining and transporting specimens from young children. sections.title: Clinical research

summary.text: Lists clinical research gaps in diagnostics, prophylaxis and treatment for children with advanced HIV disease, such as point-of-care pneumonia tests, the role of azithromycin and shorter TB preventive regimens. It also mentions ongoing studies of cryptococcal meningitis treatment that may inform care of older children.

sections.extract: Diagnostics ■Research gaps related to diagnostics in children include the need to develop simplified point- of-care diagnostics for pneumonia, specifically Pneumocystis pneumonia and cytomegalovirus disease. ■In addition, the use of rapid molecular tests in stools and other urine LAM assays needs to be further evaluated in children. summary.text: Lists ongoing operational research on paediatric TB diagnosis and prevention, such as the CaP TB programme and the TB-Speed study.

tables.notes:
ᵃ See Box 2 (11,12).

ᶜ Screening for cryptococcal antigen followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy among cryptococcal antigen–positive adolescents to prevent the development of invasive cryptococcal disease is recommended before initiating or reinitiating antiretroviral therapy for adolescents living with HIV who have a CD4 cell count <100 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation; moderate-certainty evidence) and may be considered at a higher CD4 cell count threshold of <200 cells/mm³ (conditional recommendation; moderate certainty evidence). When cryptococcal antigen screening is not available, fluconazole primary prophylaxis should be given to adolescents living with HIV who have a CD4 cell count <100 cells/mm³ (strong recommendation; moderate-certainty evidence) and may be considered at a higher CD4 cell count threshold of <200 cells/mm³ (conditional recommendation; moderate-certainty evidence). Screening and primary prophylaxis are not recommended for children younger than 10 years, given the low incidence of cryptococcal meningitis in this age group (13).

narratives.en: The table shows, for four TB preventive treatment regimens (6H, 3RH, 3HP, 1HP), whether they have a drug–drug interaction with the antiretrovirals LPV/r, EFV and DTG used in children and adolescents with HIV.
narratives.ar: يبيّن الجدول، لأربعة نظم للعلاج الوقائي من السل (6H، 3RH، 3HP، 1HP)، ما إذا كان لها تداخل دوائي مع مضادات الفيروسات القهقرية LPV/r وEFV وDTG المستخدمة لدى الأطفال والمراهقين المصابين بفيروس العوز المناعي البشري.
narratives.zh: 该表显示四种结核病预防性治疗方案（6H、3RH、3HP、1HP）是否与儿童和青少年艾滋病毒感染者使用的抗逆转录病毒药物LPV/r、EFV和DTG存在药物相互作用。
narratives.es: La tabla muestra, para cuatro pautas de tratamiento preventivo de la tuberculosis (6H, 3RH, 3HP, 1HP), si presentan interacciones farmacológicas con los antirretrovirales LPV/r, EFV y DTG utilizados en niños y adolescentes con VIH.
narratives.fr: Le tableau indique, pour quatre schémas de traitement préventif de la tuberculose (6H, 3RH, 3HP, 1HP), s’ils présentent une interaction médicamenteuse avec les antirétroviraux LPV/r, EFV et DTG utilisés chez les enfants et adolescents vivant avec le VIH.
narratives.ru: В таблице показано, имеют ли четыре схемы профилактического лечения туберкулеза (6H, 3RH, 3HP, 1HP) лекарственные взаимодействия с антиретровирусными препаратами LPV/r, EFV и DTG, применяемыми у детей и подростков с ВИЧ.

narratives.en: The table gives daily prophylactic doses of co-trimoxazole, isoniazid, the isoniazid/co-trimoxazole/vitamin B6 combination and fluconazole for children: for each drug and formulation, the recommended daily dose and the dose to give in each of seven weight bands from 3 kg to over 30 kg.
narratives.ar: يقدّم الجدول الجرعات الوقائية اليومية للأطفال من الكوتريموكسازول والإيزونيازيد والتوليفة إيزونيازيد/كوتريموكسازول/فيتامين B6 والفلوكونازول: لكل دواء وتركيبة، الجرعة اليومية الموصى بها والجرعة التي تُعطى في كل فئة من فئات الوزن السبع من 3 كغ إلى أكثر من 30 كغ.
narratives.zh: 该表给出儿童每日预防性使用复方新诺明、异烟肼、异烟肼/复方新诺明/维生素B6复方制剂和氟康唑的剂量：针对每种药物和剂型，列出推荐日剂量以及从3公斤到30公斤以上七个体重段的给药量。
narratives.es: La tabla presenta las dosis profilácticas diarias de cotrimoxazol, isoniazida, la combinación de isoniazida/cotrimoxazol/vitamina B6 y fluconazol para niños: para cada fármaco y formulación, la dosis diaria recomendada y la dosis que debe administrarse en cada una de las siete franjas de peso, desde 3 kg hasta más de 30 kg.
narratives.fr: Le tableau donne les doses prophylactiques quotidiennes de cotrimoxazole, d’isoniazide, de l’association isoniazide/cotrimoxazole/vitamine B6 et de fluconazole chez l’enfant : pour chaque médicament et formulation, la dose quotidienne recommandée et la dose à administrer dans chacune des sept tranches de poids, de 3 kg à plus de 30 kg.
narratives.ru: В таблице приведены суточные профилактические дозы котримоксазола, изониазида, комбинации изониазид/котримоксазол/витамин B6 и флуконазола для детей: для каждого препарата и лекарственной формы указаны рекомендуемая суточная доза и доза для каждой из семи весовых групп — от 3 кг до более 30 кг.

narratives.ar: يسرد الجدول الأسعار المرجعية (بالدولار الأمريكي، باستثناء النقل) ومصادر الشراء للأدوية المستخدمة في العلاج الوقائي من السل وبالكوتريموكسازول ولعلاج داء المستخفيات، يليها قسم ثانٍ للاختبارات التشخيصية.
narratives.zh: 该表列出用于结核病和复方新诺明预防性治疗以及隐球菌病的药品参考价格（美元，不含运输费）和采购来源，随后为诊断检测的第二部分。
narratives.es: La tabla enumera los precios de referencia (USD, sin transporte) y las fuentes de adquisición de los medicamentos utilizados para el tratamiento preventivo de la tuberculosis y con cotrimoxazol y para la criptococosis, seguidos de un segundo bloque para las pruebas diagnósticas.
narratives.fr: Le tableau énumère les prix de référence (USD, hors transport) et les sources d’approvisionnement des médicaments utilisés pour le traitement préventif de la tuberculose et par le cotrimoxazole et pour la cryptococcose, suivis d’un second bloc consacré aux tests diagnostiques.
narratives.ru: В таблице приведены справочные цены (в долл. США, без учета транспортировки) и источники закупок лекарственных средств для профилактического лечения туберкулеза и котримоксазолом, а также для лечения криптококкоза; за ними следует второй блок по диагностическим тестам.
